_note: Per-service enrichment used on /services/{intent}/ hubs. Each service should read genuinely different from the others - no template phrases.

upvc-windows.hubIntro: uPVC windows are the default replacement choice in the UK - roughly three quarters of homes fit them - because they're the cheapest route to an A-rated, low-maintenance frame. If your current windows are pre-2005 or anything is single-glazed, new uPVC units usually pay back in energy savings within 8-12 years.
hubBody: Frame material matters less than people expect - the glass area and the sealed unit spec drive most of the price. A standard install uses a 28mm argon-filled double-glazed unit with a warm-edge spacer and a low-E soft coat; triple glazing adds around 15% for a thermal gain that only really pays off in exposed or northern locations. Foiled finishes (Anthracite Grey, black, woodgrain) add roughly 10-20% over white.

A whole-house set of 8-10 uPVC windows is normally a 1-2 day fit by a two-person team. Insist the installer is FENSA or CERTASS registered - that self-certifies Building Regs Part L compliance, so you're not chasing separate Building Control sign-off later.
hubTips: Ask for the whole-window U-value, not just the centre-pane glass figure - a frame under 1.4 W/m²K is what you want.
Give every installer the identical brief: same units, same glazing spec, same colour, same trickle-vent requirement.
Check the guarantee covers frames and sealed units separately, and ask what happens if the firm stops trading.
Trickle vents have been mandatory on replacement windows since June 2022 - a quote without them is cutting a corner.
upvc-windows.commonSpecs: 70mm multi-chamber uPVC profile, 28mm argon-filled A-rated sealed unit, warm-edge spacer, low-E soft coat, internally beaded, multi-point locking, factory-fitted trickle vents, white or foiled finish.

double-glazing.hubIntro: Doing the whole house at once - rather than window by window over several years - gets you a single matched finish, one set of scaffolding and access costs, and usually a better per-unit price. It's the biggest glazing decision most homeowners make, and quotes for the same house can vary by thousands.
hubBody: A typical 3-bed semi runs 8-12 openings including doors, and full replacement lands somewhere between £3,000 and £9,000 depending on frame material, glazing spec, colour and how many are bay or feature windows. uPVC sits at the lower end, timber-alternative and aluminium at the top. The single biggest swing is whether any bays need structural work above them.

Whole-home jobs are where finance offers and 'today only' discounts get pushed hardest. A genuine quote holds its price for at least a week and itemises each opening so you can see what you're paying for. Walk away from anything that only works if you sign on the visit.
hubTips: Get the quote itemised opening-by-opening, not as one lump sum - it's the only way to compare fairly.
Be wary of large 'discounts' that expire the same day - the real price is the discounted one.
Confirm scaffolding, waste removal and making-good of plaster and rendering are included, not extras.
Ask for the FENSA/CERTASS certificate to be registered in your name within 30 days of completion - you'll need it when you sell.
double-glazing.commonSpecs: Matched A-rated uPVC across all openings, 28mm argon-filled units, warm-edge spacers, multi-point locking throughout, PAS 24 on doors, trickle vents to current Part F, single foiled colour inside and out.

casement-windows.hubIntro: Casement windows are the UK's default style - hinged on the side, opening outward. In uPVC they're the cheapest window to replace and the fastest to fit. If your existing frames are pre-2005 or single-glazed, A-rated casements typically pay back in energy savings within 8-12 years.
hubBody: The single biggest price driver is glass area, not the exact frame - a 1200x1200mm casement costs roughly the same in white uPVC or a basic foiled finish, but jumps for triple glazing or a flush-sash profile. Standard installs use argon-filled double glazing with a warm-edge spacer; upgrading to triple glazing adds around 15% for a marginal thermal gain in most UK climates.

Installation is usually a 1-2 day job for a whole house (6-10 windows), done by a two-person FENSA-registered team. FENSA registration matters because it self-certifies compliance with Building Regulations Part L - without it you'd need Building Control sign-off separately, which adds cost and delay.
hubTips: Ask for the whole-window U-value, not just the glass - a good frame under 1.4 W/m²K matters as much as the pane.
Get quotes on the same brief: same units, same glazing spec, same finish. Otherwise you're comparing apples and pears.
Check the guarantee covers frames and glass separately, and clarify what happens if the installer folds.
Flush-sash casements cost more than standard lipped ones - decide which look you want before you compare prices.
casement-windows.commonSpecs: Argon-filled A-rated double glazing, 28mm sealed unit, warm-edge spacer, low-E soft coat, multi-point locking, internally beaded, trickle vents (mandatory since June 2022).

bay-windows.hubIntro: Bay windows are typically the largest and most complex glazing job in a UK home - three, four or five interconnected units bridging a bay projection, often on a load-bearing wall. Getting them wrong is expensive; getting them right transforms a room and adds resale value.
hubBody: The price range on bay windows is wider than any other window type because the variables stack: 3-sided vs 5-sided, angle (usually 25° or 45°), whether the bay is squared, canted or bow-shaped, and crucially whether a structural steel is needed above. If your original bay dates from the 1930s or earlier, a steel lintel or reinforced beam is almost always required to meet current Building Regs - budget £600-£1,200 extra for structural work.

The best bay installations use a matched trio: two identical side casements plus a wider central pane (fixed or opening). Cheaper quotes sometimes hide non-matching frame widths or a plain rectangular unit dressed up as a bay - inspect drawings carefully before signing off.
hubTips: Ask to see a scaled elevation drawing before ordering - bay proportions are what make or break the look.
Confirm whether the quote includes structural work above the bay - it's a common exclusion.
Check whether the roof or apron above the bay needs re-flashing or re-tiling as part of the job.
If the bay is on a bedroom, insist on at least one opening pane large enough to meet fire escape rules (450mm min clear opening).
bay-windows.commonSpecs: 3 or 5-sided canted bay, 25° or 45° corner posts, matched frame widths, structural steel or reinforced cill where required, external lead flashing, internal decorative arch or plain reveal, argon-filled A-rated glazing.

upvc-doors.hubIntro: uPVC doors are the standard choice for back doors, French doors and patio sliders, and a budget-friendly option for the front. Most installers fit in a single day. The trade-offs versus a composite door are mainly appearance and thermal mass, not security - a decent uPVC door still takes PAS 24 multi-point locking.
hubBody: A plain uPVC panel door runs roughly half the price of a composite equivalent, and a foiled finish (Anthracite Grey is the runaway favourite) closes most of the appearance gap. Where uPVC genuinely wins is French and patio doors - a matched pair of uPVC French doors or a 2-3 pane sliding patio door is far cheaper than the aluminium alternative and performs well enough for most homes.

The locking spec is what matters. Look for a 5-point (minimum) multi-point lock, PAS 24 certification and an anti-snap, anti-bump Euro cylinder - insurers increasingly ask for all three. On patio doors, insist on anti-lift blocks and a track that won't wear out inside a decade of daily use.
hubTips: Check the door is PAS 24 certified and the cylinder is anti-snap (TS007 3-star or Sold Secure Diamond).
For a foiled colour, get a physical sample before ordering - screen photos rarely match the real finish.
On sliding patio doors, ask about the threshold height - a low or level threshold matters for accessibility and trip risk.
Confirm the glass in any door side panel is toughened or laminated to current safety-glazing rules.
upvc-doors.commonSpecs: 70mm uPVC outer frame, 28mm double-glazed or solid infill panel, 5-point multi-point locking, PAS 24 rated, anti-snap Euro cylinder, foiled or white finish, letterbox with brush and flap seal on front doors.

window-repair.hubIntro: Repair rather than full replacement makes sense when the frame is sound but a specific fault has appeared - a blown seal, a broken hinge, a misted double-glazed unit, or a mechanism that no longer closes flush. Most repairs are under £250 and done in a single visit; replacement only makes sense once repair costs approach 50% of a new window.
hubBody: The commonest fault by far is a blown seal - the sealed unit has failed and moisture has got in, showing as permanent misting between the panes. This is a glass-unit replacement, not a frame job: the existing frame stays in place, the failed unit comes out, and a new sealed unit goes in. Around £120-£180 per average unit, done in under an hour once the glass has been made to size.

The next commonest calls are for friction stays (the hinges holding a casement open), gearbox mechanisms, and cill or beading damage from historic water ingress. All are repairable in-situ for well under £200 in most cases. Anything involving a rotting timber cill or a cracked frame usually pushes past the repair-vs-replace threshold.
hubTips: Get a written diagnosis before authorising work - some 'blown seal' calls turn out to be internal condensation, which is a ventilation issue, not a glass one.
Ask how long the replacement sealed unit is guaranteed for - a decent installer will match the original 10 year seal warranty.
For urgent work (broken glass, window that won't lock), most installers charge a call-out fee of £45-£85 on top of the repair.
If more than a third of your windows have blown seals, replacement usually beats piecemeal repair - not always, but often.
window-repair.commonSpecs: Sealed unit replacement (24mm or 28mm to match), replacement friction stays, gearbox and multi-point mechanism swap, cill capping, beading replacement, hinge bolt fitting, lock cylinder upgrade.
